subject: Ops runbook: cluster layout, node slices & disk I/O considerations

Subject: Planning for on-prem Redwood Private — cluster inputs and site docs

Hi Tessa / Monica,

Thanks again for the call last week. Stately Health is moving forward with an on-prem deployment of Redwood Private for our clinical analytics pipeline. Before we lock dates with our data center, we want a compact runbook from the Redwood team that covers: cluster layout (control plane sizing, worker pools), storage classes and recommended backing (NVMe vs SAN vs Ceph), network egress/ingress expectations, and disk I/O guidance for mixed real-time and batch workloads.

Attached are our current rack layout and the site power/cooling spreadsheet. A few notes from our infra team: peak concurrent requests to the inference API are expected to be ~350 qps for short bursts (3–5 min) with a baseline of 40 qps; model context lengths average 2048 tokens; retention for request logs is 30 days, and all PHI must remain in our VPC (no egress).

Could you provide: 1) a compact checklist for cluster prep, 2) node pool recommendations (counts/instance types or equivalent), and 3) storage performance targets (IOPS, latency) and PVC reclaim policy suggestions? We'd like to review internally on Wed 17 Feb.

Attachments: rack-layout-v2.pdf (application/pdf), site-power-and-cooling.xlsx (application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet)

Appreciate it — let me know if you want a quick pairing session with our DC ops.

Best,
Alex Morton
VP, Platform Engineering
Stately Health Systems

From: markus_klein <markus_klein@redwoodinference.com>
To: tessa_morgan <tessa_morgan@redwoodinference.com>, monica_patel <monica_patel@redwoodinference.com>, Alex Morton <alex.morton@statelyhealth.com>

Subject: Re: Planning for on-prem Redwood Private — cluster inputs and site docs

Alex / team — quick technical write-up below. I focused on node slices (separation of concerns), storage tiers, and disk I/O targets given your workload notes (model context ~2048, bursts to 350 qps).

1) Cluster topology (high level)
- Control plane: 3 dedicated control-plane nodes (VM or baremetal) in separate racks if possible. Each: 16 vCPU, 64GB RAM, 500GB NVMe for etcd and kubelet (fast local storage for etcd snapshots).
- Etcd/storage IO: prefer local NVMe as primary for etcd disk; replicate snapshots to your SAN/backups. Ensure clock sync / NTP and stable power for these nodes.

2) Node pools (suggested separation)
- gpu-serving-pool: 6 nodes (A40 or equivalent) — primary model inference. Each: 48 vCPU, 512GB RAM, 2 x 1TB NVMe local (for KV cache + transient caches), 1 x 10GbE redundant NIC.
- cpu-burst-pool: 4 nodes (CPU-only) — burst CPU workloads, preprocessing, async batches. Each: 32 vCPU, 256GB RAM, 1TB SSD (network-backed or NVMe).
- infra-pool: 3 nodes (m4/m5 equivalent) — logging, metrics, control-plane proxies, ingress. Each: 16 vCPU, 64GB RAM.
- storage-backend: 3 nodes running Ceph OSDs (if you choose distributed storage) — prefer 4 x NVMe per OSD node for high IOPS, or connect to existing SAN if present.

Notes: counts above are starting points for your stated baseline/burst profile. If guidance on model sizes (params) changes, GPU count should be adjusted. For strict latency SLOs, add 1–2 spare hot-standby serving nodes to the gpu-serving-pool for failover.

3) Storage classes & performance targets
- fast-ssd (local NVMe): for KV cache, model weights staging, and etcd (where sub-10ms latency is required). Target: 50k–100k IOPS per node (NVMe), 99th p99 latency <5ms for small reads.
- balanced-block (replicated Ceph or SAN with SSD tier): for persistent model artifacts and bulk traces. Target: 5k–20k IOPS, p99 <20ms.
- archive (object store): for long-term request logs and artifacts (S3-compatible).

PVC reclaim policy: set Retain for model artifacts and logs you need to preserve across node rebuilds; set Delete for ephemeral cache PVCs. For example: KV caches: Delete; model staging: Retain (back up via scheduled job).

4) Disk I/O considerations and caching
- Use local NVMe for cache layers to avoid network hop for hot KV accesses. Keep write amplification low by using ext4/XFS tuned for low latency; enable discard and appropriate scheduler (noop or mq-deadline depending on kernel).
- Provide an LVM layer only if you need dynamic resizing; otherwise bind-mount NVMe partitions for predictable performance.
- If you have a SAN only, ensure it can sustain 200–300k aggregate IOPS during bursts; otherwise plan for hybrid approach (local NVMe for hot cache + SAN for longer-term).

5) Network & egress gating
- Ensure private connectivity between serving nodes and model storage (no public egress). Use VPC routing or dedicated VLANs and enforce ACLs at the top-of-rack.
- Reserve 25Gbps aggregate for GPU-serving-pool interconnects if models stream large contexts frequently.

6) Operational tips
- Deploy a small (1–2 node) KV cache warmers to reduce cold-start latency after reboots.
- Add a pre-flight script to validate NVMe health and SMART before node allocation.
- Backup strategy: etcd snapshots daily and upload to a secure S3 bucket in a separate network segment.

Attachments referenced: disk-benchmark.csv (we should run a fio profile: 4K random read/write, 70/30 r/w, 16k depth to simulate KV behavior).

If you want, I can convert these into a short runbook checklist and a table of node types vs cost/throughput.

— Markus Klein
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
